newsitem.title: FRANCE: ONIC head justifies higher wheat export target.
newsitem.headline: ONIC head justifies higher wheat export target.

text.p: France has export commitments for 5.4 million tonnes of soft wheat for the world market so far this season, of which 3.28 million have already been shipped, French cereals office ONIC said on Wednesday.
Director general Alain Moulinier said these sales justified ONIC's decision to raise its export goal to 6.25 million tonnes in the year to June 30 from the 6.0 million target previously projected.

Speaking a a press conference, he declined to say where demand for the remaining 850,000 tonnes would come from and called the figure a reasonable estimate despite signs that attention would soon turn to the next crop.
"We are at the stage when people start to look at the new crop but having said that, during this campaign we have seen that we can get the volumes out," he said.
"We do think we can do more than six million," he said.
Several industry analysts continue to project French exports outside the European Union at six million tonnes or less.
Egypt, now the world's largest importer, recently bought half a million tonnes of French wheat but this is likely to be one of the last major deals for old-crop, analysts have said.

France also sold 600,000 tonnes of wheat to Iraq in December and January under a United Nations oil-for-food pact though none has yet been shipped. A small volume of wheat shipped to Iraq is believed to be linked to other food aid programmes.

The EU as a whole has issued export commitments of some seven million tonnes for commercial soft wheat grain so far this season. It has until around May to reach a probable export target of nine to 10 million tonnes, before the 1996/97 campaign effectively merges into the next crop, traders say.
The official crop campaign runs from July 1 to June 30.
EU export licences for open-market grain can be used to ship from anywhere in the 15-nation bloc, but ONIC seeks to estimate how much of the grain will in practice come from France.
Moulinier said the EU's export pace was "relatively in line with our predictions at the start of the season," but declined to say whether Brussels should now speed things up further.
He played down the threat of friction between Europe and the United States over grain export subsidies, saying both sides had the right to give out the aid within Uruguay Round limits.

U.S. farm leaders have called for dormant U.S. subsidies to be brought out again, while Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman warned this week that the EU aid could not go on forever without a response from Washington.
